title: Turning the condition around
objectives: Find $P(B \mid A)$ from $P(A \mid B)$, and see that the two differ
Derive Bayes' rule from the multiplication rule

screens.title: Turning the condition around
screens.prose: A test catches most people who are ill. So does a positive result mean you are probably ill? We will see why the answer depends on which way round you ask.
A clinic screens 100 people for an illness. The diagram sorts them by two facts: ill or not, and a positive test or not.
screens.question: What share of the ill people test positive?

widget.label: Share of the ill who test positive

hints.text: How many people are ill in all?
The left circle holds every ill person: 2 plus 8.
10 people are ill, and 8 of them test positive. Divide 8 by 10.

feedback.correct: 8 of the 10 ill people test positive.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Keep only the ill people, then count the positives among them.

byKey.whole: You divided by all 100 people. The question keeps only the 10 who are ill.
byKey.pos: You divided by the 26 people who tested positive. The question keeps the ill people, so divide by 10.
byKey.ill-share: That is the share of everyone who is ill. Among the ill, count those who test positive.

explain.text: You kept the 10 ill people and found 8 positives among them. We write this $P(+ \mid \text{ill}) = 0.8$. The test catches most ill people.

screens.prose: Now turn it around. You are told only that a person tested positive. Find everyone that could be.
screens.question: Tap every region that holds people with a positive test.

hints.text: Which circle is the positive test?
The right-hand circle holds every positive test, overlap included.

feedback.correct: 26 people tested positive: 8 ill and 18 well.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap both parts of the right-hand circle, and nothing else.

byKey.ill: You tapped the ill people. This time the group is everyone with a positive test.
byKey.only-both: You tapped only the overlap. The 18 well people with a positive test are positive too.
byKey.A: That part holds ill people whose test was negative. They are not in the positive group.
byKey.none: The outside holds people who are neither ill nor positive.

explain.text: You tapped the overlap and the rest of the right-hand circle: $8 + 18 = 26$ people. Those 26 are the new whole we count inside.

screens.prose: We write $P(\text{ill} \mid +)$ for the chance of being ill **given** a positive test. The two events have swapped sides of the bar.
screens.question: What is $P(\text{ill} \mid +)$? Give a fraction or a decimal.

hints.text: Count inside the 26 positive people only.
The overlap holds the positives who are ill.
8 of the 26 positives are ill. Divide 8 by 26.

feedback.correct: 8 of the 26 positives are ill, about 0.31.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the ill positives by everyone who tested positive.

byKey.inverse: That is $P(+ \mid \text{ill})$ from the first screen. Now the group is the positives, not the ill.
byKey.whole: You divided by all 100 people. Only the 26 positives are left.
byKey.well: You counted the 18 well positives. The question asks for the ill ones.

explain.text: Same overlap of 8, a different whole: 8 out of 10 one way, 8 out of 26 the other. So $P(+ \mid \text{ill}) = 0.8$ but $P(\text{ill} \mid +) \approx 0.31$. Turning the condition around changes the answer.

screens.prose: Usually nobody hands you the counts. You get rates. 10% of people are ill. The test is positive for 80% of the ill and 20% of the well.
screens.question: What is $P(\text{ill} \cap +)$, the chance a person is ill and tests positive?

hints.text: Follow the path Illness, then Positive.
Multiply the two chances on this path.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply the chances along the path Illness, then Positive.

byKey.added: You added the two chances on the path. A path multiplies them.
byKey.sens: That is the chance of a positive given ill. You still need to weight it by how many are ill.
byKey.base: That is the chance of being ill. Only 80% of the ill go on to test positive.

explain.text: You multiplied along the path: $0.1 \times 0.8 = 0.08$. That is 8 people in 100, the overlap from the diagram.

screens.prose: Same tree. A positive test can come from an ill person or from a well one.
screens.question: What is $P(+)$, the chance a random person tests positive?

hints.text: How many paths end in a positive test?
Two paths end in a positive test.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply along each path that ends in a positive, then add them.

byKey.ill-only: You counted only the ill path. Well people test positive too, on 20% of tests.
byKey.add-rates: You added 0.8 and 0.2 without weighting them. Most people are well, so weight each rate by its group.
byKey.average: You averaged 0.8 and 0.2. The well group is nine times larger, so the rates need weights.

explain.text: Two paths end in a positive: $0.08 + 0.18 = 0.26$. That is the 26 positives in 100 people.

screens.prose: You have both pieces now: the ill-and-positive path, and all the positive paths.
screens.question: So what is $P(\text{ill} \mid +)$?

options.why: That is ill and positive together. Divide it by the chance of any positive, 0.26.
That is the share of positives who are well. You want the ill path on top.
You divided by $P(\text{ill})$, which gives $P(+ \mid \text{ill})$ again. The condition is the positive test.

hints.text: Which path is the one you want, and which paths make up the condition?
The condition is a positive test: both highlighted paths.
Divide the ill-and-positive path, 0.08, by both positive paths, 0.26.

feedback.correct: 0.08 out of 0.26, the same as 8 out of 26.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the path you want over every path into the condition.

explain.text: You divided the ill-and-positive path by all the positive paths: $0.08 / 0.26 \approx 0.31$. It matches the count of 8 out of 26.

screens.prose: A different test. Its leaflet says it is positive for 90% of ill patients. A doctor tells a patient with a positive result he is 90% likely to be ill.
screens.question: Using the tree, what is the patient's real chance of being ill?

options.why: That is $P(+ \mid \text{ill})$, the leaflet's number. The patient needs $P(\text{ill} \mid +)$.
That is ill and positive together. Divide it by all the positives, $0.18 + 0.24$.
That is the chance before the test. A positive result should move it.

hints.text: Which paths end in a positive test?
Positives come from both of these paths.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the ill-and-positive path by every positive path.

byKey.inverse: You took the leaflet's 90% as the patient's chance, as the doctor did. That is the chance of a positive given illness: the condition the wrong way round.

explain.text: Positives come from two paths: 0.18 from the ill and 0.24 from the well. So $P(\text{ill} \mid +) = 0.18 / 0.42 = \tfrac{3}{7} \approx 0.43$, not 0.9. Swapping the condition like the doctor is called the inverse fallacy.

screens.prose: Each time you put one path over all the paths into the evidence. That recipe is **Bayes' rule**. It comes from writing $P(A \cap B)$ two ways.
screens.question: Put the lines of the derivation in order. Start with the line that contains $P(B \mid A)$.

lines.text: $P(A \cap B) = P(B \mid A)\,P(A)$: the multiplication rule, going through $A$ first
$P(A \cap B) = P(A \mid B)\,P(B)$: the same event, going through $B$ first
$P(B \mid A)\,P(A) = P(A \mid B)\,P(B)$: both lines equal $P(A \cap B)$
$P(B \mid A) = \dfrac{P(A \mid B)\,P(B)}{P(A)}$: divide both sides by $P(A)$, which is not 0

hints.text: Which line sets the two products equal? It needs both products first.
The last line is the only one with $P(B \mid A)$ alone on the left.
Write $P(A \cap B)$ through $A$, then through $B$. Set the two equal, then divide by $P(A)$.

feedback.correct: Two ways to the same event, set equal, then divided.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $P(A \cap B)$ both ways before you set them equal.

byKey.d3: Setting the products equal needs both of them written first.
byKey.d4: Dividing by $P(A)$ is the last step: it isolates $P(B \mid A)$.

explain.text: $P(A \cap B)$ is one path, and we can reach it through $A$ or through $B$. Setting the two products equal and dividing gives $P(B \mid A) = \dfrac{P(A \mid B)\,P(B)}{P(A)}$. The bottom, $P(A)$, is every path into $A$ added up, as on the tree.

screens.prose: A trading signal fires on 80% of up days and 30% of down days. Over the past years, 55% of days were up days. Today the signal fired.
screens.question: What is the chance today is an up day? Give a decimal.

widget.label: Chance of an up day given the signal

hints.text: Which two paths end with the signal firing?
These two paths end with the signal firing.
$0.55 \times 0.8 = 0.44$ and $0.45 \times 0.3 = 0.135$. Divide 0.44 by their sum.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put the up-and-fires path over both paths where the signal fires.

byKey.inverse: That is the chance the signal fires on an up day. You want the chance of an up day when it fires.
byKey.joint: That is up and firing together. Divide by every way the signal fires, 0.575.
byKey.prior: That is the share of up days before the signal. The signal should move it.
byKey.fires: That is the chance the signal fires at all. It belongs on the bottom of the fraction.

explain.text: Up and firing is $0.55 \times 0.8 = 0.44$; down and firing is $0.45 \times 0.3 = 0.135$. So $P(\text{up} \mid \text{signal}) = 0.44 / 0.575 \approx 0.765$. An 80% hit rate does not mean the signal is right 80% of the time it fires.

ideas: $P(+ \mid \text{ill})$ and $P(\text{ill} \mid +)$ share a top but divide by different groups, so they usually differ.
To turn a condition around, put the path you want over every path into the evidence.
The two directions agree when the two events are equally likely, and usually not otherwise.

formula.name: Bayes' rule
formula.note: The bottom is every path into $A$: $P(A) = P(A \mid B)P(B) + P(A \mid B^c)P(B^c)$.

summary.trap: A test that catches 90% of the ill does not make a positive 90% likely to be right. That swap is the inverse fallacy.

quiz.prose: One card is drawn from a standard 52-card deck. Every king is a face card, so $P(\text{face card} \mid \text{king}) = 1$.
quiz.question: What is $P(\text{king} \mid \text{face card})$?

options.why: That is $P(\text{face card} \mid \text{king})$. Turned around, the group is the 12 face cards, and only 4 are kings.
You divided by the whole deck. Only the 12 face cards are left.
You split the face cards by suit. Count kings among jacks, queens and kings: 4 of 12.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the kings among the face cards.

explain.text: There are 12 face cards: four jacks, four queens and four kings. So $P(\text{king} \mid \text{face card}) = \tfrac{4}{12} = \tfrac{1}{3}$, while $P(\text{face card} \mid \text{king}) = 1$.

quiz.question: What is $P(A \mid B)$? Give a decimal.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $P(A \mid B) = P(B \mid A)\,P(A) / P(B)$.

byKey.inverse: That is $P(B \mid A)$, the condition the other way round.
byKey.joint: That is $P(A \cap B)$. Divide it by $P(B)$.
byKey.upside: You swapped $P(A)$ and $P(B)$. Multiply by $P(A)$ and divide by $P(B)$.

quiz.prose: Events $A$ and $B$ are equally likely: $P(A) = P(B) = 0.25$. You also know $P(A \mid B) = 0.6$.
quiz.question: What is $P(B \mid A)$?

options.why: You took $1 - 0.6$. Turning a condition around is not a complement.
You multiplied by $P(B)$ but did not divide by $P(A)$.
Bayes' rule needs $P(A \mid B)$, $P(B)$ and $P(A)$, and you have all three.

feedback.correct: When $P(A) = P(B)$, the two conditionals are equal.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Apply Bayes' rule with these numbers.

explain.text: $P(B \mid A) = P(A \mid B)\,P(B) / P(A) = 0.6 \times 0.25 / 0.25 = 0.6$. The two directions agree only when the two events are equally likely.

quiz.prose: A bank's report says: “90% of fraudulent card payments are made abroad.”
quiz.question: Which probability is 0.9?

options.why: That turns the condition around. The report starts from the fraudulent payments and asks where they were made.
The 90% is a share of fraudulent payments, not of all payments.

feedback.correct: The group is fraudulent payments; abroad is what we count in it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask which group the 90% is a share of.

explain.text: “Of fraudulent payments, 90% are abroad” fixes fraud as the condition. So it is $P(\text{abroad} \mid \text{fraud}) = 0.9$. Most payments abroad may still be genuine.
